story: In 2008, astrophysicists examining NASA's WMAP satellite data uncovered an anomaly that rattled cosmology: hundreds of galaxy clusters were streaming across space at nearly two million miles per hour. Even stranger, they were all moving in the same uniform direction toward a patch of sky between Centaurus and Vela. This motion, dubbed dark flow, was completely independent of the universe's expansion. Because standard physics dictates that galaxies should move randomly relative to the cosmic microwave background, lead researcher Alexander Kashlinsky proposed a staggering explanation: massive structures lying beyond our observable universe were gravitationally pulling our cosmos. Some theorists even suggested the pull came from a sibling universe in a multiverse. Though follow-up data from the European Space Agency's Planck satellite failed to confirm the flow—leading many scientists to dismiss it as a statistical fluke—the mystery of dark flow remains one of astronomy's most chilling debates.
angle: Hundreds of massive galaxy clusters were caught rushing at 2 million miles per hour toward a single point beyond the edge of our observable universe, suggesting an unseen cosmic titan—or another universe—is pulling them.
disputed: Existence of Dark Flow: Mainstream cosmology and Planck satellite data indicate dark flow is not statistically significant and likely a data artifact, while Kashlinsky's team maintains it is real. Script should attribute dark flow as a claimed discovery rather than proven fact.

Planck Data Interpretation: The official Planck collaboration found no bulk flow, whereas team member Fernando Atrio-Barandela argued alternate filtering confirmed it. Script should attribute Atrio-Barandela's viewpoint as a minority re-analysis.
Multiverse Pull: Theories connecting dark flow to sibling universes (Mersini-Houghton) are speculative. Script should frame multiverse claims as 'proposed by some theoretical physicists'.
